extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and practitioners of climatology, physical geography, and agriculture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for characterizing the atmosphere and climate (composition, pressure, heat distribution, humidity, electricity) and for relating climatic data to vegetation and agricultural suitability. Includes observational methods, mapping conventions (isothermal/isotheral/isochimenal lines), causal factors, and applied thresholds for cultivation (e.g., vine/wine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric composition (quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A volume of dry air contains 20.8 of oxygen, and 79.2 of nitrogen, besides from two to five thousandth parts of carbonic acid gas, a still smaller quantity of carbureted hydrogen gas, and traces of ammoniacal vapors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chemical analysis (Dumas and Boussingault) sets the baseline composition; footnotes cite Boussingault, Lewy, and Liebig for more precise locality measurements (e.g., Audilly carbonic acid proportion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxygen variation is slight
rubrics_metrics.description: Some observations of Lewy render it probable that the quantity of oxygen varies perceptibly but slightly, over the sea and in the interior of continents, according to local conditions or to the seasons of the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small variations may occur due to biological activity (e.g., microscopic organisms affecting dissolved oxygen in sea, with consequent alteration of adjacent air strata). See Lewy's Comptes Rendus article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of atmospheric carbonic acid (CO2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources from which carbonic acid may be yielded to the atmosphere include the respiration of animals, supply from the interior of the earth near exhausted volcanoes and thermal springs, decomposition of carbureted hydrogen gas in the atmosphere, and electric discharges of clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant nightly exhalation is not counted here because daytime plant respiration counterbalances it; see Boussingault and Liebig for agricultural/physiological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental noxious admixtures (miasmata) hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the normal constituents, there are accidental admixtures, especially near the ground, which in the form of miasmatic and gaseous contagia may exercise a noxious influence on animal organization; their chemical nature has not yet been ascertained by direct analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferred from decay processes and pathology analogies — possible constituents include ammoniacal and other nitrogenous vapors, sulphureted hydrogen gas, and polybasic ternary and quaternary compounds analogous to vegetable combinations; these may produce miasmata associated with ague and typhus fever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosols and suspended particulates (dust, infusoria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winds and currents caused by ground heating can carry solid substances reduced to a fine powder to considerable elevations; dust that darkens the air and falls on distant islands contains silicious-shelled infusoria (Ehrenberg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such suspended solids affect atmospheric transparency and can be transported over long distances (Darwin's observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal features for a descriptive picture of the atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated principal features: (1) Variations of atmospheric pressure; (2) Climatic distribution of heat; (3) The distribution of the humidity of the atmosphere; (4) The electric condition of the atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four dimensions form the main axes for describing atmospheric state and for comparative climatology; the text develops each in turn with observational and causal detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations of atmospheric pressure (including horary oscillations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations of atmospheric pressure include horary oscillations with regularity in the tropics (producing an ebb and flow), differences according to latitude, season, and elevation, and important accidental fluctuations often attendant with violence and danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horary oscillations are highly regular in the tropics (barometer can indicate hour within ~15–17 minutes); their amplitude diminishes from equator to high latitudes; barometric behavior should be compared with wind direction, temperature alternations, and humidity. See observational references (Humboldt, Bouvard, Bravais, Martins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Climatic distribution of heat (isothermal framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Climatic distribution of heat depends on the relative position of transparent and opaque surface masses and hypsometrical configuration of continents, determining isothermal lines (curves of equal mean annual temperature) horizontally and vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use isothermal, isotheral (equal summer), and isochimenal (equal winter) lines to map comparative climatology; the inflections of these lines reveal the influence of land/sea distribution, elevation, and surface properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of atmospheric humidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative relations of humidity depend on differences in solid and oceanic surfaces, distance from the equator, level of the sea, form of precipitation, and the connection between deposits, temperature changes, and wind patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humidity mapping must consider precipitation forms and seasonality and be related to temperature and wind observations for accurate interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric condition of the atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric condition (primary cause when skies are serene is contested) includes relation of ascending vapors to electric charge and cloud form, periodicity by day and year, zonal differences, frequency of thunderstorms, and causal connections to hail, water and sand spouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate cloud formation, electric tension, and the influence of ascending vapors; refer to research by Peltier and others on spout phenomena and seasonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometric windroses as an analytical tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of atmospheric pressure during different winds, termed 'barometric windroses', afford deeper insight into the connection of meteorological phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use windrose tables to correlate pressure patterns with prevailing winds and derive climatic inferences; see Leopold von Buch's work on barometrische windrose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of rotation and opposing upper/lower currents (Dove)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dove's 'law of rotation' in both hemispheres explains many atmospheric processes: opposing upper currents (polar eastward deflection, equatorial westward deflection) produce great phenomena of pressure, warming/cooling, precipitation, and cloud formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the law of rotation to interpret wind deflection, the descent of upper currents, cloud figures, and general weather patterns; see Dove's Meteorologische Untersuchungen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition of polar and equatorial currents as causal framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference of temperature between equatorial and polar regions engenders two opposite currents in upper strata and on the Earth's surface; their places of descent and displacement determine major meteorological phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate locations where upper currents descend to the formation and appearance of clouds and to resultant surface weather; cloud shapes can indicate upper-region processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and regional knowledge of monsoons and seasonal winds
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsoons and land/sea winds are controlled by radiation differences and periodic variations in the sun's declination; knowledge of these winds dates back millennia in Hindostan, China, and Malayan regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical, local knowledge along with physical theory to understand large-scale seasonal wind systems; etymology and regional names reflect seasonality (e.g., 'mausim').

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of long-term, widely distributed observations (magnetic/meteorological stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chain of 'magnetic stations' and long series of observations across long distances will be of immense importance in determining the 'law of the winds' and deciding whether currents originate centrally or descend from higher regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative observations spanning many hundreds of miles and continued for more than twenty years are needed for dependable conclusions about prevailing winds and currents; Mahlmann's calculations support middle-latitude west-southwest prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isothermal / isotheral / isochimenal lines — mapping distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Isothermal (equal annual), isotheral (equal summer), and isochimenal (equal winter) lines are distinct and not parallel; inflections arise from surface heterogeneity and modify agricultural/vegetational limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot separate seasonal isotherms when assessing cultivation limits; net agricultural effect depends on seasonal distribution of temperature, not only annual mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes that raise mean annual temperature (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes that 'raise' temperature include: proximity of a western coast in the temperate zone; divided continental configuration (peninsulas, bays); position relative to polar ice or extensive continental land under the same meridian; prevailing southerly/westerly winds on western shores; mountain chains acting as protective walls; infrequency of swamps; absence of woods on dry sandy soils; constant summer serenity of the sky; vicinity of a warm oceanic current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these factors collectively when interpreting isothermal inflections and local climatic warmth advantages for cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes that lower mean annual temperature (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes that 'lower' temperature include: elevation above sea-level (if not on a broad plain); vicinity of an eastern coast in mid/high latitudes; compact continental configuration; extension of land toward polar ice without intervening open sea; mountain chains obstructing warm winds; isolated peaks causing cold downslope currents; extensive woods (evaporation, shade, radiation); prevalence of swamps; cloudy summers; very clear winters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these depressing influences when assessing limits of cultivation, winter severity, and isothermal concavities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade winds' influence on temperate zone winds and coast climates
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade winds (easterly winds within the tropics) give rise, in temperate zones, to prevailing west or west-southwest winds which are land winds to eastern coasts and sea winds to western coasts; east winds of the continent tend to be cooler than west winds unless modified by ocean currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this relation to explain east–west coastal temperature contrasts and their effects on local climate and agriculture (citing Forster, Dove, Kämtz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insular versus continental climate contrast ('excessive' continental climates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seas moderate temperatures leading to insular/littoral climates; interiors of large continents exhibit 'excessive' climates (great summer heat and severe winter cold), with large differences in mean temperatures and seasonal extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contrasts influence vegetation, agriculture, transparency of atmosphere, and elevation of perpetual snow-line; cite examples (Tobolsk, Irkutsk vs Berlin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct versus diffused light as factor in plant ripening
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between direct and diffused light (clear versus overcast skies) affects 'unmeasured' heat locally developed in living vegetable cells and materially influences ripening and color of fruits independently of thermometer-indicated temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photometric/optical conditions should be considered alongside thermometric readings when assessing suitability for crops; Humboldt urged physicists and physiologists to attend to this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermic scale of cultivation (plant heat requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thermic scale orders crops (vanilla, cacao, banana, cocoa-nut → pine-apples → sugar-cane → coffee → date-trees → cotton → citrons → olives → chestnuts → vines/wines) and indicates that limits of cultivation depend on multiple climatic relations, not solely mean annual temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map cultivation limits using seasonal temperatures, radiation quality, humidity, and other local factors rather than only annual means; refer to Humboldt and Meyen for detailed plant geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold cited for producing 'potable' wine (vine cultivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'potable' wine it is requisite that the mean annual heat should exceed 49 degrees, that the winter temperature upward of 64 degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an illustrative rule in Humboldt's discussion and is accompanied by tabulated examples comparing places (Bordeaux, Strasbourg, Berlin, etc.); interpret with caution and local context (note possible textual ambiguity regarding the second figure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal distribution of temperature matters more than coarse annual comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of mean annual temperature between regions (e.g., America vs Europe) are often meaningless without separate comparison of winter and summer temperatures and an analysis of seasonal distribution, which is crucial for agriculture, industry, and human comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always analyze seasonal (winter/summer/spring/autumn) means and specific months (e.g., effect of late May frosts on flowering) when assessing climatic suitability.
